Trikala Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Trikala, Greece

Not demolished. Jews probably lived in Trikala since antiquity, though the Ottomans expelled the community to Istanbul in 1453; by 1506, about 90 Jews had returned, forming a small Romaniot community that absorbed Spanish, Portuguese, Sicilian, and (1526) Hungarian refugees, becoming predominantly Sephardi and peaking around 1,000 by the late 17th century across three congregations (Romaniot, Sephardi, Sicilian), each with its own synagogue - two burned in 1749, with one rebuilt. Greek annexation in 1881 granted religious freedom; a 1906 Zionist organization was the first of several in following years. By the 1920s, the community maintained two synagogues, a school, two welfare organizations, and a theater company. Population reached 520 by 1940, though only a quarter survived the war, with many deported to death camps. Following German withdrawal in 1944, Jews gradually returned, numbering 267 by 1945, reestablishing a small community. This cemetery's founding is unknown, presumed 16th century.
